title: Wayyiqtol

objectives.can: Recognise a wayyiqtol form, parse it, and read it as the next event of a narrative.

explanation.summary: Most Hebrew stories are told with one verb form, the wayyiqtol: a yiqtol-type verb with וַ in front and a doubled first consonant. It is the commonest verb form in the Hebrew Bible. Learn to spot it and a page of narrative falls into a line of events.

sections.heading: What the form looks like
body: A wayyiqtol verb begins with the syllable וַ (waw with pataḥ). The prefix consonant of the yiqtol that follows is normally doubled, which shows as a dagesh. So the prefix of the third masculine singular, yod, appears with a dagesh in וַיִּקַּח, and the prefix of the third feminine singular, tav, appears with a dagesh in וַתֹּאמֶר. The person, gender and number are carried by the same prefixes and endings as in the yiqtol, and the analysed text records them in the same way.

Two things change this picture. First, the guttural א cannot take a dagesh. With the first person singular (prefix א) the pataḥ of וַ is therefore lengthened to qamets, and the form begins וָאֶ or וָאֹ, as in וָאֹמַר. Second, before a yod with shewa the doubling is given up, as in וַיְהִי.
Because the analysed text counts the וַ as part of the verb, the whole word is one wayyiqtol form. The English 'and' is not a separate word to look for.

sections.heading: A yiqtol that is often shorter
body: The verb after וַ looks like a yiqtol, but where the root allows it, it is a shorter form with the stress drawn back toward the beginning of the word. Compare the plain yiqtol and the wayyiqtol of the same verb:

sections.heading: What it does in a story
body: In narrative the wayyiqtol usually presents events one after another: this happened, and then that, and then that. A chain of them is the main line of a story. In Ruth 1:1 two wayyiqtols, 'it was' and 'he went', carry the story to its first action, and the chain continues through the next verses.

The form וַיְהִי, 'and it happened', very often opens an episode, with a time expression after it. English tends to translate each wayyiqtol as a simple past ('he went', 'she died'), and that is the usual sense in narrative. But the form is not itself defined as 'past tense', and the sequence it shows is often a sequence of telling rather than strict time. A later lesson looks at what stands off the main line.

sections.heading: Why a form like this? Two explanations
body: What you can observe is the shape described above and the way it is used. Why the form exists is a question grammarians answer differently, and the answers are explanations, not facts.

The older explanation, found in the traditional grammars, says that the prefix וַ is a 'waw conversive' or 'consecutive' that turns an imperfect verb into a narrative past. A later explanation, common in historical grammars, sees in the shortened form a very old past tense with a short prefix, which survived in this one construction, with wa- as a connecting particle. You will meet both ways of speaking. This course teaches the form by its shape and its use and does not ask you to choose between them.

misunderstandings: A yiqtol with the ordinary conjunction וְ is not a wayyiqtol. The wayyiqtol has pataḥ under the waw and a dagesh in the next letter (וַיֹּאמֶר), and the ordinary conjunction does not.
Not every past event in a story is a wayyiqtol. Background, earlier events and descriptions are often given with other forms. Wayyiqtol is the form of the main line, not of the past as such.
Do not translate every wayyiqtol with 'and then'. The English 'and' is usually enough, and the order of the clauses is often all that shows the order of events.
A wayyiqtol is not always third person. First person (וָאֹמַר, 'and I said') is common in speeches and accounts told in the first person.

deeper.heading: Wayyiqtol outside plain narrative
body: Besides telling a story, wayyiqtol is also used in other kinds of text, for example in historical summaries, and in a few passages where it describes a habit or a result. Grammarians list these uses at length. For reading the stories of Genesis, Ruth and Samuel, the rule 'next event in the main line' will carry you most of the way.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: AND IT came to pass in the days when the judges judged, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Beth-lehem in Judah went to sojourn in the field of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three wayyiqtols in Qal. וַיְהִי stands twice, once to set the time ('in the days when the judges judged') and once to introduce the famine. The prefix is yod with shewa, so there is no doubling. וַיֵּלֶךְ, 'and he went', has the doubled yod and moves the story into action: this is where the main line of the book begins.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Elimelech Naomi's husband died; and she was left, and her two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַיָּמָת, 'and he died', is a wayyiqtol of the root מוּת with the stress drawn back. וַתִּשָּׁאֵר is a wayyiqtol too, but in the Niphal and feminine singular (tav doubled): 'and she was left'. The two events follow one another and the second is a result of the first.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And it came to pass after these things, that God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַיְהִי opens the whole episode, 'and it happened after these things'. Two wayyiqtols of the root אָמַר follow, each וַיֹּאמֶר, 'and he said': first God speaks to Abraham and then Abraham answers. The same form introduces the speaker each time the speaker changes.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son; and he cleaved the wood for the burnt-offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Six wayyiqtols in one verse, one for each step of Abraham's early start: he rose early (Hiphil), saddled, took, split the wood (Piel), arose, went. The chain gives the events in the order of telling, and the verse is a good picture of what a wayyiqtol sequence looks like on the page.

reading.why: The first five verses of Ruth are the story of a family told almost entirely in wayyiqtol: a journey, two deaths, two marriages. They show the chain at work.
